sources.title: Uncovering the Valleys Hidden Below Greenland’s Ice

items.title: Greenland's Bedrock Valleys, Now Mapped More Sharply Than Before
items.body: Below the Greenland Ice Sheet lies a landscape no human eye has directly seen. NASA's Earth Observatory reports that a newly developed method for mapping that hidden bedrock has produced the most detailed and accurate view of it yet, revealing an expansive network of valleys carved into the surface beneath the ice. The value of a map like this is that it turns a blank in the human record into terrain: a surface with shape and direction, inferred rather than visited. The ice sheet is what people look at; the valleys are what sits underneath it.

sources.title: The ICJ prepares a landmark ruling on the Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar

items.title: Why The Gambia Is the Country Suing Myanmar
items.body: The International Court of Justice is reportedly set to rule in the coming weeks in The Gambia v. Myanmar, the genocide case against Myanmar. The unusual part is the applicant: The Gambia is not the country where the alleged violations occurred, and it has no obvious national stake of its own in the outcome. Under international law, that does not disqualify it — any state can file a case at the ICJ if it believes a country has violated the convention. Myanmar tried to shut the case down on jurisdictional grounds, and in a 2022 decision the court rejected that attempt. That permission is doing a great deal of work: it is why a country with no direct connection can ask the court to rule on another government's conduct.

sources.title: Guest Contribution: “Oligarchy is a Symptom, Not the Cause”

items.title: Not Every Real Problem Is the Root Cause
items.body: In a guest contribution at Econbrowser, Jeffrey Frankel — the Harpel Professor at Harvard's Kennedy School of Government — starts from the observation that many factors are at play in American politics, a long list that includes things crying out for reform, such as gerrymandering of congressional districts. His caution concerns what happens next. Most of those factors, he writes, will not bear the weight of being identified as the single fundamental exogenous cause of all the others. The distinction is worth keeping: real problems and root causes are different categories, and a long list of the former can feel like an answer without actually functioning as one.

sources.title: Coyote killed in Cape Breton Highlands National Park, but closures still in place

items.title: A Coyote Was Killed in Cape Breton Highlands. The Closures Remain.
items.body: Parks Canada says staff have killed a coyote in the MacIntosh Brook area of Cape Breton Highlands National Park, after a camper was bitten earlier in the week and temporary closures were put in place in parts of the park. The agency says it is not clear whether the coyote killed is the same one responsible for the bite.

sources.title: Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll

discussion.body: Nine separate questions, plus immigration, and nearly half of Albertans still haven't picked a side. That's a large pool of voters, not a settled verdict.
Undecided early on isn't the same as persuadable. It can mean people simply haven't started paying attention yet — and 'softening' can describe anything from warmer feelings to cooler ones.

items.title: Nearly Half of Albertans Still Haven't Decided on Nine Referendum Questions, CBC-Commissioned Poll Suggests
items.body: A new poll commissioned by CBC News suggests Albertans are divided over immigration — though the outlet reports attitudes are softening — and that nearly half of respondents still don't know which way they'll vote on the nine non-separation questions in the Oct. 19 referendum. The undecided figure is the more striking one: a split electorate on immigration is a familiar story, but a large bloc with no position at all, three weeks out, is a different problem for anyone trying to read the result in advance.

sources.title: Supreme Court vote shadows Maine Sen. Susan Collins in her first race after abortion rights decision

items.title: Susan Collins Faces Her First Ballot Since the Decision That Overturned Roe
items.body: PBS NewsHour notes that the Nov. 3 election will be the first time Susan Collins has appeared on a ballot since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that overturned Roe v. Wade, a decision PBS says resulted in abortion being banned in much of the United States. Her previous appearance on a ballot predates that ruling — so this is the first time voters weigh her under the new legal landscape rather than the old one.

sources.title: Watch: Shipwreck uncovered on Nantucket island during nor'easter storm

items.title: A Nor'easter Washes Up What May Be a 19th-Century Shipwreck in Massachusetts
items.body: A nor'easter has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, according to local media reports relayed by the BBC. The tentative wording is doing real work: something a storm drags out of the shoreline is a candidate for identification, not a solved case.

sources.title: Healey to promise 'new age of industrialisation' for UK in conference speech

items.title: UK Chancellor Picks Shipbuilding as the Sector to Spotlight at Labour's Conference
items.body: The chancellor will unveil policies aimed at boosting British shipbuilding in his speech to Labour's annual conference on Monday, the BBC reports. Party conferences are where a government names its priorities out loud; the instruments that follow the naming are the part a speech alone can't settle.

sources.title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Assassin(s)’ and ‘Tazza 4’ Dominate Chuseok Holiday Weekend Surge

items.title: A Hur Jin-ho Thriller Led Korea's Chuseok Box Office Surge
items.body:
Director Hur Jin-ho's political crime thriller "The Assassin(s)" topped the South Korean box office over the weekend of Sept. 25–27, according to KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council.

It opened into a major surge across the peak Chuseok festival frame — a holiday window that compresses moviegoing into a few days, giving a newly opened local film a kind of attention an ordinary weekend can't match.

sources.title: Chris Rock Says Infidelity and Struggling to ‘Make It’ Aren’t Just Hollywood Problems: ‘If You Got No Love, You’re Broke as F—k’

discussion.body: There's built-in comedy in a performer with Rock's tenure making a film about how punishing the pursuit of stardom is. The punchline is implied before anyone writes a script.

Or the more generous reading: the mockery is aimed at the rituals — the comeback machinery, the optics — rather than at anyone who wants the career in the first place. The film can laugh at the trappings while still taking the wanting seriously.

items.title: What Chris Rock's 'Misty Green' Is Actually Satirizing
items.body:
Rock's new film "Misty Green" centers on a fictional actress, played by Rosalind Eleazar, mounting a Hollywood comeback after years in a fading career. Misty's journey pokes fun at the trappings of trying to "make it" in the entertainment industry — a pursuit Rock himself is rejecting after his decades-spanning career.

The distinction is worth noticing: the joke isn't only on the gatekeepers who decide who gets a second act. It's on the chase itself, which is a less flattering premise for an industry story than the usual talent-deserves-a-break plot.

sources.title: Conservatives propose eliminating tax on diesel sales until Canada Day

items.title: Poilievre's Diesel Plan Reaches All the Way to the Carbon Tax
items.body:
Pierre Poilievre advocates removing all diesel production taxes by permanently scrapping two federal measures: the industrial carbon tax and the Clean Fuel Standard.

The scope is the telling part. Both named instruments sit on the production side, so the proposal concerns what fuel makers pay rather than a number set directly at the pump — and whether any relief travels downstream to drivers is a separate argument from whether the taxes come off the books.

sources.title: Civil rights enforcement cuts mean fewer staff, closed offices, longer waits for students with disabilities

items.title: A Federal Complaint Line That Parents Relied On Is No Longer the Same Resource
items.body:
Filing a civil rights complaint with the Office of Civil Rights can be parents' last stop when a school dispute runs out of other options. Following cuts and restructuring, that federal office is no longer serving as the same resource.

An enforcement office's usefulness is partly a matter of capacity: a complaint route is only as real as the staff able to act on what arrives. The reported narrowing touches families whose remaining options were already thin.

sources.title: ‘Carrie’ Cast Guide: Who Plays Who In The Latest Adaptation Of Stephen King’s Debut Horror Novel

items.title: A New 'Carrie' Puts Summer H. Howell in the Telekinetic Prom Queen's Shoes
items.body: Deadline's cast guide for Prime Video's Carrie places Summer H. Howell in the title role — the telekinetic prom queen, a part the guide credits Sissy Spacek with originating. The series comes from Mike Flanagan and adapts Stephen King's debut horror novel, with all episodes premiering Oct. 7. Deadline frames the project as Carrie White taking another form after 50 years, which is one way of saying the story has now outlived several of the actors who made it famous. A retelling of something this familiar is rarely about what happens; it is about what the new version decides to look at, and how long it is willing to wait before the blood drops.

sources.title: ‘Lanterns’ Review: Episode 7 Changes ‘The Jordan Boys’ Legacy — and Sets Up a Charged Finish

discussion.body: The portals and dead worlds are the easy part — they can be rendered. A bond that matures late is riskier, because it depends on the audience having noticed the earlier distance.
Or the late bond is the safe part. Cosmic imagery is what a penultimate episode is expected to deliver; two leads finally getting along is the cheapest way to make an hour feel consequential.

items.title: 'Lanterns' Reaches the River Styx, Then Asks What the Partnership Is For
items.body: IndieWire's review of the penultimate episode of Lanterns Season 1 describes an hour stuffed with cosmic furniture: dark matter portals, dead alien worlds, and a dangerous ride across the river Styx. The critic's argument is that the spectacle is not what stays with you. What lingers, in that reading, is what becomes of Hal and John's late-maturing bond — a relationship that took most of a season to arrive at something worth watching. That is a harder trick than a portal. Mythic set dressing can be borrowed from anywhere; a partnership that only clicks in the final stretch has to be earned by everything the show did while it was not clicking.

sources.title: Victims of Quebec helicopter crash remembered as TSB launches probe

items.title: Four Die in a Quebec Helicopter Crash, With the Fire's Timing Still Unresolved
items.body: A helicopter crashed in Quebec on Saturday, killing four people. It is not yet known whether a fire erupted before the crash or after it — a sequencing question that matters for understanding what happened in the air and what happened on the ground.

sources.title: ‘Musk’ Producer, Atwater-Magnific Exec & ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Director Talk AI: “It’s Important To Get In The Driver’s Seat” – Zurich Summit

discussion.body: The accidental pairing is the best part of the lineup. You could not cast a more loaded double bill than 'Musk' and 'AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About' for a conversation about AI in film.
Credits are not arguments. A producer of one film and a director of another arrive with whatever views they hold, and the titles tell us nothing about what anyone on that panel actually said.

Fair, but the composition still hints at the shape of these industry conversations: with Atwater Capital's founder seated alongside the filmmakers, the discussion likely slides from craft toward cost and ownership.

items.title: The Zurich Summit's AI Panel Included a Producer of 'Musk' and the Director of 'AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About'
items.body: At the Zurich Summit this weekend, producer Nick Shumaker sat on a panel digging into what AI means for film. Also on stage: Hollywood film financier Vania Schlogel, and directors Zack London and Nick Holt, whose credits include 'Gods Don't Give Gifts' and 'AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About' respectively. Schlogel is founder and managing partner of L.A.-based Atwater Capital, which puts a fund manager's chair at the table next to the filmmakers' ones — a reminder that the AI question in Hollywood is tangled up with who finances and owns the output, not just which tools get used on set. The panel billing itself is almost a joke: a producer of 'Musk' and the maker of a film whose title shrugs off the whole subject, sharing a stage to discuss the subject seriously.
